newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Competition rules do not cover pollution surveillance firms.
newsitem.headline: Competition rules do not cover pollution surveillance firms.

text.p: The European Court of Justice said on Thursday competition rules do not apply to private companies hired by public authorites to carry out anti-pollution surveillance schemes.

The court distinguished a state's exercise of an official duty, to enforce environmental protection rules, from instances where it carries on economic activities by offering goods or services on the market, and found no reason the port authority could not hire a private company to carry out its duty to observe the loading and unloading of acetone products.
This case was brought to an Italian court by a shipper of oil, Diego Cali, who refused to pay anti-pollution surveillance charges to a private company engaged by the port of Genoa.
Cali claimed charges levied against it by a private company amounted to an abuse of a dominant position by the environmental firm, but the court disagreed.

"Such surveillance is connected by its nature, its aim and ...the exercise of powers relating to the protection of the environment which are typically those of a public authority. It is not of an economic nature justifying the application of the treaty rules on competition," the court said.
(Court translation into English. Original language of the case: Italian)
"Harbour company - Prevention of pollution - Legal monopoly - Abuse of a dominant position"
Reference to the court from the Tribuanale di Genova (Italy) for a preliminary ruling in the proceedings pending before that court between
Servizi Ecologici Porto di Genova SpA (SEPG)
on the interpretation of article 86 of the EC Treaty

Article 86 of the EC Treaty must be interpreted as not being applicable to anti-pollution surveillance with which a body governed by a private law has been entrusted by the public authorities in an oil port of a member state, even where port users must pay dues to finance that activity.
